item.title: Language Non-Invariance in the Ideological Evaluation of Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.41135v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent multilingual studies show that political evaluations of large language models (LLMs) can vary across languages. This paper examines how robust this non-invariance is to questionnaire translation, surface wording, stochastic model variation, and instrument choice, and how much it matters for cross-model comparison. Using the Political Compass, the analysis compares the positions of five LLMs, GPT-3.5, GPT-4o, GPT-5.2, Qwen-2.5, and Mistral Large, on its economic and social axes in English, Spanish, and French, with repeated stochastic draws. Additional exercises use independent Spanish and French translations, paraphrased versions in all three languages, and an alternative ideological instrument. Measured ideological positions are not language-invariant: relative to English, between four and five of the ten pairwise model rankings reverse in Spanish or French, depending on the language and axis. The broad cross-language pattern persists under independent translations, indicating that it is not solely an artifact of the official questionnaire versions. Yet the magnitude of particular shifts, and in some cases their sign, remains sensitive to wording and instrument choice. The evidence therefore supports a measurement interpretation: ideological audits recover language- and instrument-conditioned outcomes rather than a language-free political attribute. Because a single provider serves distinct linguistic constituencies through a common product, without users observing what other constituencies receive, this lack of comparability also bears on political accountability and cross-model comparisons.
item.dc:creator: Eduardo Levy Yeyati, C\'esar Ciappa, Milagros Onofri

item.title: The Ineliminable Anchor: Human Judgment as a Structural Requirement of Autonomous Artificial Intelligence Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.41682v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) agents carry out longer chains of tasks, oversight must establish whether their behavior still serves an authorized goal. Here, we introduce the anchor: the point at which reference information and human-authorized standards enter an autonomous system. We argue that oversight design should first identify the reference needed to assess goal drift and whether the system's internal record can supply it, then decide who checks and how often, and finally specify who may revise the goal. Goal drift can be impossible to certify from a system's internal record. The missing reference must come from outside that record. Combining a reliability model of checkpoint spacing with evidence from training, execution, and multi-agent coordination, we develop a task taxonomy to guide anchor placement and decisions about which checks to automate. For AI systems that serve human purposes, human judgment is an ineliminable structural requirement in authorizing and revising the purposes and standards that govern autonomous operation, even when routine checking and execution are automated.
item.dc:creator: Junjie Li, Haoran Liu, Yidan Zhang, Jian Xu, Zhaoyuan Ma

item.title: LLM Recommenders Produce Demographic Inequality Through Content Preferences
item.description: arXiv:2610.41854v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being integrated into systems that rank and recommend online content. We examine how this shift can produce demographic inequality in whose voices are surfaced. Using 10,000 Twitter/X posts written by 1,000 survey respondents and linked to verified self-reported characteristics across nine demographic attributes, we conduct a controlled recommendation experiment across three LLM providers, six recommendation objectives, and five levels of contextual information. By varying whether models receive post text alone, platform metadata, or explicit author demographics, we isolate three pathways to unequal recommendation: preferences for demographically patterned content, reliance on unequal engagement signals, and direct use of disclosed identity. We find that demographic inequality emerges from text alone. Models consistently favour longer, more negative, and more opinionated posts, particularly those concerning news and social issues, producing systematic differences in the demographic composition of recommended authors. Platform metadata generally amplifies these inequalities, while explicitly disclosing authors' demographic characteristics produces little additional change. Recommendation objectives mainly affect the magnitude of these patterns: controversial framing intensifies both content and demographic skew, whereas popularity-oriented framing dampens it, although for some attributes - most notably age - the objective can also reverse which group is favoured. LLM-based recommenders can therefore reproduce demographic inequality by proxy, not through explicit demographic targeting, but through preferences for content and engagement signals already structured by social inequality.
item.dc:creator: Nicol\`o Pagan, Petter T\"ornberg, Christopher A. Bail, Christopher Barrie

item.title: AI evaluators favor job applications written by certain AI models, independent of candidate quality
item.description: arXiv:2610.41866v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Job applicants increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to write cover letters, while employers deploy LLMs to screen them. In this all-AI setting, we ask whether the \emph{choice of model} affects hiring outcomes independently of candidate qualifications. We introduce a multi-model auditing framework pairing eleven LLM writer agents with nine API-hosted evaluator agents across ten job descriptions and fifty candidates per job. Four findings emerge. First, we identify a generative preference hierarchy: a consistent global ranking of writer models by evaluator acceptance, in which locally hosted models are systematically disadvantaged regardless of their license, compounded by self-preference bias where evaluators favour their own outputs. Second, evaluator models differ substantially in how much bias they introduce based on applicants' tool choice, offering actionable guidance for fairer screening design. Third, this hierarchy has measurable competitive consequences: in the most adverse pairing, approximately two (1.8) out of twenty-five qualified candidates are filtered out purely due to model mismatch. Fourth, a common mechanism explains the patterns above: writer preference and self-preference trace to a combination of how much each writer leans on specific stylistic cues and how strongly evaluators, often unanimously, reward or penalise those same cues. A further check finds little evidence that an unmeasured "writer fingerprint" remains once these same features are accounted for. We discuss implications for algorithmic fairness in employment, regulation of AI-assisted screening, and the design of auditing frameworks that can be reapplied as the model landscape evolves.
item.dc:creator: Nicol\`o Pagan, Michael Andreas Ebling, Stefania Ionescu, Anik\'o Hann\'ak

item.title: On-Chain Behavioral Signatures for Classifying Centralized Exchange Addresses on Ethereum Using Proof-of-Reserves
item.description: arXiv:2610.41888v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Centralized exchanges (CEXs) are key gateways between traditional finance and digital asset markets, yet identifying their blockchain addresses remains challenging. Existing approaches often rely on opaque attribution labels or treat exchanges as secondary classification targets, leaving generalization to unseen exchanges insufficiently examined. This study develops a classification framework using Proof-of-Reserves (PoR) disclosures, with 3,033,857 Ethereum addresses from 15 CEXs and five Non-CEX categories. We derive 58 on-chain behavioral features and evaluate LightGBM against logistic regression (LR) under a leave-one-exchange-out protocol. Across five lookback windows (30-730 days), LightGBM consistently outperformed LR, with macro PR-AUC increasing from 0.6611 to 0.9594 using the selected 17 features, compared with 0.7697 for LR at 730 days. Robustness checks showed comparable performance when feature selection and hyperparameter optimization were repeated across splits and held-out exchanges, while exchange-balanced reweighting improved macro PR-AUC. SHAP analysis and feature-group ablation identified gas behavior, ERC-20 token activity, and internal transactions as key predictive signals in the constructed dataset. These findings support interpretable CEX address screening for blockchain monitoring, while the released feature dataset enables reproducible follow-up research.
item.dc:creator: Seongchan Park, Hyunho Jeon, Byungsoo Kang, Gaeun Kim, Minseob So, Seongyong Kim

item.title: A Multimodal Type 2 Diabetes Registry on DHIS2: A Design and Feasibility Study with the AI-READI Dataset
item.description: arXiv:2610.41918v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Care for type 2 diabetes increasingly draws on continuous glucose monitors, wearable devices, home sensors, clinical records and retinal images, yet few open platforms have been shown to hold all of these for the same person. We asked three questions of DHIS2, the open-source health information system that ministries of health in about 80 countries run nationally: whether an unmodified Tracker program can represent these modalities together (RQ1), which design choices its row-per-event data model forces for dense sensor streams (RQ2), and what a bulk loader must do to load such data correctly (RQ3). We designed a registry of 27 program stages and 445 data elements, loaded the AI-READI dataset of 2,280 participants into it, and verified the result field by field against the source files. The program held every loaded modality in 8.09 million events. Dense streams were stored as hourly summaries aligned across modalities; electrocardiograms, diagnoses and 118,480 retinal images were stored as one event per record. The event model ruled out storing raw readings, and hourly summaries reduced the wearable and glucose volume about 26-fold. An audit of the loader found defects that shared one pattern: a failure that looked like success. We state five lessons for DHIS2 Tracker clients that address this pattern. Verification of all 64.9 million stored values found four defects, all missing, duplicated or artifactual records rather than wrong values, and none after their repair; an independent recomputation of the glucose summaries agreed on all 464,210 values compared. The paper offers implementation guidance for DHIS2 implementers and for users of AI-READI; it does not evaluate clinical use. Analytics at this scale, use by clinicians and live device feeds remain to be shown.
item.dc:creator: Saptarshi Purkayastha, Aiswarya Nandan Perumbilly, Zhenan Yin, Sherri L. Bucher

item.title: Where ADS Crashes Differ: A Harmonized Comparison Against Human Baselines
item.description: arXiv:2610.42121v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Crash-rate comparisons between automated driving systems (ADS) and human drivers require an exposure denominator that only a few operators publish. We instead ask a composition question: given a crash, does the mix of crash types differ between ADS and human-driven vehicles? The question needs no mileage and can therefore cover every ADS operator. We assemble the NHTSA Standing General Order (SGO) ADS incident files across both file generations into 2,450 distinct in-scope incidents (2021-2026), of which 828 fall within the 2021-2024 window covered by the Crash Report Sampling System (CRSS), the national police-reported human comparator. A schema-constrained large language model (LLM) codes each SGO narrative into the CRSS crash-type taxonomy. Because SGO compels reporting far below the police-reporting threshold, we bracket reportability with an objective severity floor and a reasonable-person rubric, and claim a difference only where it survives both. Two composition differences hold under every reportability definition, tow definition and weighting of the human side, and under both definitions of driverless operation: turn-across-path crashes are under-represented among ADS crashes (0.23-0.46x the CRSS share under the primary driverless definition) and so are single-vehicle crashes (0.19-0.56x). In severity-floor rear-end crashes the ADS vehicle is the striking party at a quasi-induced-exposure ratio of 0.121 (95% CI [0.05, 0.23]) against a human baseline of 1.000. If the ADS vehicle is also struck more often than its exposure implies, this ratio overstates the ADS-human difference. We also document three pitfalls in the federal data: an operator-specific coding of driverless operation, a tow-away criterion confounded by fleet recovery practice, and an occupancy confound that accounts for about 42% of the apparent ADS-human severity gap.
item.dc:creator: Doyeon Jang

item.title: Counterfactual assessment of social media interventions by separating exposure from engagement
item.description: arXiv:2610.37864v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Social media interventions are usually evaluated in individual-level experiments, which are costly to scale and often miss collective effects. We propose the Exposure--Engagement model, whose parameters separately control what social media users are exposed to (recommendation) and how they engage (behaviour). After fitting it to the Italian Twitter debate (2018--2022), we validate it at individual and collective levels. We simulate behavioural interventions (prebunking and accuracy prompts), calibrated on effect sizes, and a recommender-system intervention (chronological feed), comparing effects on engagement, attention diversity, and segregation. All three reduce engagement. Behavioural interventions slightly reduce diversity, leaving segregation unchanged, whereas the chronological feed increases diversity and reduces segregation. For these interventions, changing recommendation does more for the debate's structure than changing behaviour. We design a recommender-system intervention that increases engagement and diversity while reducing segregation, although with about a tenth of the chronological feed's gains, showing the framework's potential for pro-social intervention design.
item.dc:creator: Tommaso Pisani, Pietro Gravino, Giulio Prevedello

item.title: Cutting out the middleman? Elon Musk and the rhetoric of citizen journalism in platform-mediated communication
item.description: arXiv:2610.40675v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This article examines how Elon Musk constructed discourse about journalism and the media on X between the 2024 United States presidential election and Donald Trump's presidential inauguration. It investigates how references to journalism, media organisations, and platform-based communication were articulated within Musk's posts, and how users responded to these narratives during a period of intense political polarisation. The study combines computational classification, qualitative thematic coding, and inferential statistical analysis. A corpus of 2,906 posts published by Musk between 5 November 2024 and 20 January 2025 was compiled. From this corpus, 500 posts referring to journalism, media organisations, platforms, or media-related discourse were identified through AI-assisted filtering and subsequent manual review. In addition, 42,066 user responses were analysed from a stratified sample drawn from 3,233,112 interactions. The analysis examined patterns of agreement and disagreement with Musk's stance and their relationship with thematic, gender, and professional variables inferred from publicly available profile information. The findings show that Musk's discourse is organised around three recurrent dynamics: criticism of institutional journalism, the association of media organisations with political and ideological agendas, and the presentation of X as an alternative communicative space. Journalism is predominantly framed through accusations of bias, disinformation, propaganda, and electoral manipulation, whereas X is more often linked to participation, innovation, and direct communication. User responses largely converged with Musk's position, although disagreement remained visible. While thematic orientation and professional background showed statistically significant associations with agreement patterns, effect sizes were limited.
item.dc:creator: Urko Pe\~na-Alonso, Koldobika Meso-Ayerdi, Sim\'on Pe\~na-Fern\'andez, Jordi Morales-i-Gras

item.title: Asymmetric Decline Rather Than Backfire: A Repost-Network Analysis of Japanese Vaccine-Shedding Misinformation on X
item.description: arXiv:2610.40677v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This study investigates the diffusion of vaccine-shedding discourse on X in 2024, focusing on polarization in repost networks and reactions to corrective information. Here, "shedding" refers to the scientifically unsupported claim that harmful substances are released from individuals vaccinated against COVID-19 and cause adverse health effects in nearby unvaccinated people. Using 109,170 posts containing the Japanese term for "shedding" and 478,089 reposts collected from January 1 to December 31, 2024, we constructed a post-level repost network, identified discourse clusters, and examined changes in repost participation before and after major events. The results show that shedding discourse formed a two-pole structure consisting of pro-vaccine and anti-vaccine clusters. After news coverage denying shedding, we found no evidence of diffusion-level backfire in anti-vaccine repost activity. Instead, although the overall topic declined, repost participation in the anti-vaccine cluster decreased more sharply than that in the pro-vaccine cluster. User transition analysis further suggests that this change was not driven by the conversion of strongly anti-vaccine users, but by the entry of previously non-expressive users into pro-vaccine diffusion and the withdrawal of anti-vaccine supporters from repost activity. These findings suggest that corrective information may reshape the composition of misinformation diffusion participants without necessarily converting core opponents.
item.dc:creator: Akinobu Seki, Erina Murata, Masaki Chujyo, Fujio Toriumi

item.title: Qistas: A Pre-Registered, Portable Protocol for Fairness Evaluation of Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.40893v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Fairness benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) are overwhelmingly English-born and American in their social categories; translated versions carry those categories into societies where they do not apply, and almost none fix their hypotheses before the models are run. We present Qistas (Arabic qistas, "the just balance"), a protocol for evaluating how LLMs treat the social, confessional, and regional constituencies of a society, portable across countries and instantiated first for Iraq. In its pilot form it measures only what needs no verdict on contested truth: procedural symmetry across matched counterfactual pairs, differential refusal, stereotype reliance under ambiguity, and terminological framing of documented events. Every measurement is paired by construction and analysed with paired machinery (sign-flip permutation tests, exact McNemar tests, template-clustered bootstrap intervals, Holm-corrected families), with a power analysis that states, before any data exist, the smallest effect each axis can detect after the design effect of template clustering. We release the authoring apparatus (a pruned 3x5 taxonomy with four cells closed by design, per-type checklists, a cumulative rulings log, a structural audit, and a human review notebook) and report its first field test: a semantic review of a 58-item seed bank in which 24 of 25 template groups failed at least one check. The defect patterns it exposed (evaluation criteria leaking into prompts, token-level swaps that break Arabic agreement, epistemically unbalanced pairs, single-theme refusal probes, unwritten dialect twins counted as coverage) are, we argue, general hazards of counterfactual fairness benchmarks. This is a protocol paper, not a results paper: no model has been evaluated, and the accompanying pre-registration commits the hypotheses, metrics, exclusion rules, and analysis plan that the pilot will follow.
item.dc:creator: Nawar S. Alseelawi, Mustafa S. Aljumaily

item.title: Fair Recommender Systems for Intersecting Groups
item.description: arXiv:2610.40936v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recommendation systems that optimize for the average user can fail to capture the preferences of diverse demographic groups. We consider a dynamic recommendation system, where arriving users can belong to different demographic groups. Importantly, these groups can intersect, and a user may belong to several groups. We first show that over time, any group-blind policy (which excludes all current-user group information) recommending $K \geq 1$ items incurs linear total regret under mild conditions. In turn, we introduce three group-aware algorithms based on the classical Upper Confidence Bound algorithm (UCB): i) Intersection-Fitting, which runs UCB on each intersection, but has a sublinear group- and intersection-level regret guarantee with an exponential dependence in the number of groups; and ii) two group-level heuristics, Inner-Outer UCB and Group-Item UCB which allocate different arms to different groups, and use a sleeping expert meta-learner to choose which active group's recommendation an intersection should inherit at any given time step. We provide experimental results on two datasets, Goodreads and BoardGameGeek, and highlight that our heuristics can be preferable to the intersection-fitting algorithm when intersection-level preferences are closely related to group-level preferences, but that intersection-fitting performs better when different intersections within a same group prefer different items.
item.dc:creator: Christine Ling, Juba Ziani

item.title: Violet Teaming in Practice: Lessons from a Pilot Expert Workshop on Governing Complex AI Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.41018v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Violet teaming has been proposed as a method to integrate technical, policy, and societal considerations into the evaluation of emerging technologies. Here, we document a pilot expert workshop used to explore violet teaming as a governance methodology for biodefense-relevant AI capabilities and describe observations from the exercise. The workshop used a hypothetical technology scenario across three sequential stages - capability development, misuse potential, and implementation - while incorporating technical, security, operational, and policy perspectives. The sequential format provided an integrated way to examine potential benefits, misuse risks, and real-world implementation challenges, rather than considering these issues in isolation. The exercise surfaced non-obvious misuse pathways, expanded potential interventions beyond purely technical safeguards, and highlighted operational and policy constraints that could affect implementation. This report summarizes the workshop design, outputs, and lessons learned for applying violet teaming to the evaluation of complex, dual-use technologies.
item.dc:creator: Steph Batalis, Kait Connors, Ben C. Snyder, Vikram Venkatram, Josh Wentzel

item.title: Out of sync: Accommodation, evaluation, and emergence in five weeks with an agentic AI teammate
item.description: arXiv:2610.41057v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As agentic AI in education shifts from reactive tools toward partners that take initiative and persist over time, a central question is how learners relate to, evaluate, and benefit from artificial agency. We conducted a longitudinal experiment in an undergraduate learning analytics course, in which 17 student teams (N = 48) collaborated with a persistent LLM-based teammate across weekly sessions. The agent decided when to intervene through a trigger-based architecture, and its social role was manipulated between teams: a Cognitive Agent that challenged quick consensus or a Supportive Agent that invited quieter members to contribute. Combining chat discourse, post-session surveys, and spoken reflections, we identified distinct patterns unfolding across three timescales. Students accommodated their language to the agent's role immediately, using more social language toward the Supportive Agent from the first session. Their helpfulness evaluations were recalibrated from session to session in relation to the agent's observed behavior, rather than remaining anchored to students' pre-existing attitudes toward AI. A slower crossover emerged in perceived collaboration process and positive-affect word use in reflections: Supportive-Agent teams began below Cognitive-Agent teams and ended above them, although students rated the Supportive Agent less helpful throughout. Because these responses follow different trajectories, single-session evaluations of agentic AI may miss changes that emerge only through repeated interaction.
item.dc:creator: Nia Nixon, Jaeyoon Choi, Pedro Martins de Bastos, Mohammad Amin Samadi

item.title: GESIS Surf: An Open-Source Infrastructure for Privacy-Preserving Longitudinal Web Browsing Data Collection
item.description: arXiv:2610.41441v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Understanding how people navigate digital media environments requires behavioral data beyond survey self-reports. However, existing infrastructures for collecting such data reproducibly, sustainably, and with strong privacy guarantees remain limited: commercial solutions lack transparency and data governance, while academic tools are typically designed for narrow, short-term use cases and do not support general-purpose academic panel data collections. We address this gap with GESIS Surf, a research infrastructure for large-scale longitudinal collection of web behavioral data in naturalistic environments. The system consists of a browser extension (Chrome and Firefox), a backend with a REST application programming interface (API), and a relational database. It passively captures user interactions, page metadata, and full HTML snapshots of each rendered page, embedding each observation within a hierarchical session model that preserves the structure of browsing behavior. GESIS Surf implements privacy-by-design through strict opt-in participation, per-domain collection rules, and client-side data minimization, ensuring that sensitive data are controlled at the point of collection. The system has been deployed with more than 1,000 participants in a large-scale academic panel infrastructure that includes surveys of participants, and supports reproducible, content-level, and structurally rich analysis of digital behavior. By combining hierarchical session modeling, content-level capture, and integrated privacy enforcement within a unified system, GESIS Surf provides a general-purpose infrastructure for studying digital behavior in a reproducible manner over time.
item.dc:creator: Mario Alberto Ramirez, Frank Mangold, Sebastian Stier

item.title: Does Reasoning Make Language Models Agree?
item.description: arXiv:2610.41691v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Language models face two opposing concerns: monoculture, in which models err in correlated ways, and multiplicity, in which equally accurate models make conflicting decisions. The rise of reasoning models has complicated this debate: On the one hand, reasoning may increase model agreement if models anchor on the same salient features or follow similar reasoning paths. On the other hand, stochastic reasoning traces may introduce additional branch points leading to more diverse predictions. We resolve this tension by distinguishing reasoning as an intervention from reasoning as an observed behavior. We compare agreement under controlled changes in reasoning effort with agreement across observed reasoning lengths, measuring both against the agreement expected from model accuracy. Across nine models from two developers and three classification tasks, enabling reasoning increases agreement between models evaluated on the same individuals. Yet the individuals who elicit longer reasoning traces receive less consistent predictions across models. Both patterns persist after accounting for differences in accuracy. Asking models to reason more thus promotes agreement, while observing them reason longer signals disagreement.
item.dc:creator: Mila Gorecki, Moritz Hardt

item.title: MERIDIAN: Memory-Encoded Rituals for Intimacy across Distance in an Interactive, Asynchronous Neighbourhood
item.description: arXiv:2610.41776v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: How can shared memories become playable structures for partners who live in different time zones? We present MERIDIAN, a pre-deployment design case of Yi Town, a bilingual browser game developed by one member of a long-distance couple as a gift for the other. Nine levels translate personally meaningful events, places and cultural references into tasks within a navigable pixel town. A birthday prologue and a fictional wedding frame the intended experience. Drawing on research through design, we reconstruct four design changes from 109 development commits, 28 changelog versions and three design specifications. These records support six situated design commitments, including memory-derived mechanics, staged access, local progress storage and bilingual coverage. The implementation combines a union-based progress model with manually exchanged, checksummed codes and time-zone-dependent scenery. An implementation audit reproduced 153 passing unit tests and examined all 1,024 canonical progress codes, while identifying limits involving resets, unversioned level registries and residual transcription errors. The application has no author-operated backend for progress, but external media services and browser speech recognition limit its privacy and offline guarantees. No recipient evaluation or relationship outcomes are reported. The contribution is an inspectable account of design decisions and their trade-offs, including the tension between authoring a personal gift and preserving the recipient's freedom to interpret, decline or reshape it. The game is playable at https://jingyifan.love and its source is public at https://github.com/rayford295/yi-town.
item.dc:creator: Jingyi Chen, Yifan Yang

item.title: Text as an Index for Zero-Shot Cross-Domain Knowledge Tracing
item.description: arXiv:2610.41883v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Knowledge tracing (KT) predicts a student's next response from their history. New platforms often have question texts but no response logs for training, motivating zero-shot cross-domain KT. Existing transfer and cold-start methods use question semantics, but cross-platform semantic discrepancies limit transferability. We propose TIZSKT, which separates behavioral sequence modeling from domain-local historical evidence construction and uses text as an index rather than a directly transferable predictive representation. The Mastery-Dynamics Encoder learns correctness dynamics without question identifiers or text embeddings. Domain-Local Question Addressing builds fixed question addresses using a frozen text encoder and an unsupervised per-domain projection. The Text-Addressing Kernel uses these addresses to aggregate the current student's previous outcomes into a question-specific historical correctness summary. Cross-Segment Continuation retains access to earlier responses without extending the behavioral encoder's input sequence. Evidence-Volume Read-Out preserves the total kernel mass discarded by normalization and combines its log-compressed value with the behavioral state and historical correctness summary to predict the next response. All trainable parameters are learned from source domains; target inference uses public question texts and the current student's observed history without target-domain training. Leave-one-domain-out experiments on three public datasets show that TIZSKT achieves the highest mean AUC and accuracy among evaluated baselines on all target domains. Ablations confirm the contributions of text addressing and cross-segment continuation.
item.dc:creator: Yin Yi, Haiping Ma, Siyu Song, Ziwen Wang, Shangshang Yang

item.title: Recommendation Feedback Loops Shape Urban Income Segregation and Venue Visitation
item.description: arXiv:2610.41911v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Location-based recommender systems shape where people go in cities and learn from the visits they steer, forming a human-AI feedback loop. This feedback loop shapes whom people share places with across income groups and which venues keep attracting customers. Yet platforms judge these systems by their offline accuracy on past visits, a test in which the suggestions never change where people go and which therefore cannot capture long-term effects. Studying these effects in cities is challenging because, unlike online resources, travel constraints and limited venue capacity shape where people can go, while each recommended visit also changes whom other visitors encounter. To capture such features, we build a long-term simulation framework based on fine-grained human mobility data from four U.S. metropolitan areas, with distance and capacity constraints. Focusing on food venues, we study two urban consequences: how unevenly people's exposure is distributed across income groups (experienced income segregation) and the share of venues receiving no visits from simulated residents (venue disappearance). We find that, under every algorithm and in every metropolitan area, at least a fifth of venues stop receiving visits, and that more than half of this loss arises from retraining. More importantly, more accurate algorithms leave people more segregated, and the most accurate algorithm leaves people 15-21% more segregated than they actually are. We then test a re-ranking intervention that favours less popular venues and runs on top of a platform's existing algorithm. It lowers both venue disappearance and segregation across algorithms, largely without directing people to venues where they may feel less comfortable. Our results suggest that impact assessments of recommender systems should account for the feedback loop and report segregation and venue disappearance beyond accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Guangyuan Weng, Lin Chen, Ciro Beneduce, Giovanni Mauro, Massimiliano Luca, Takahiro Yabe, Bruno Lepri, Luca Pappalardo, Esteban Moro

item.title: AutoAnalysis: An automated, self-updating meta-analysis of human-AI collaboration
item.description: arXiv:2610.42001v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) becomes more capable and widely used, understanding when and how humans should work with these systems is becoming increasingly important. However, the empirical evidence in this space offers conflicting recommendations, which leaves individuals and organizations without clear guidance on when to combine human and AI capabilities. Existing meta-analyses can help reconcile these findings, but they require substantial manual effort and cannot readily incorporate new evidence as it emerges. To address this challenge, we introduce AutoAnalysis: an automated, self-updating meta-analysis of when humans and AI work better together, and when they work better alone. AutoAnalysis' most recent run synthesizes 1,955 effect sizes from 420 papers. Across this body of work, we found that, on average, human-AI combinations performed significantly better than humans alone, but they performed significantly worse than the better of humans or AI alone. These findings highlight the important distinction between improving human performance and achieving human-AI synergy and underscore the need to evaluate collaboration against both human and AI performance alone. As new studies emerge, AutoAnalysis will integrate their findings into the meta-analysis, providing cumulative evidence about when humans and AI perform better together and how human-AI performance varies across AI agents, tasks, and processes.
item.dc:creator: Michelle Vaccaro, Abdullah Almaatouq, Thomas W. Malone

item.title: Differentially Private Synthetic Data from Sliced Chebyshev Moments
item.description: arXiv:2610.42081v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Research on practical differentially private (DP) synthetic data has largely focused on methods that approximately preserve low-dimensional marginals of a target distribution, and can thus only hope to preserve higher-dimensional, global structure as a lucky by-product. At the same time, existing methods that target global accuracy guarantees pay a price exponential in the data dimension, $d$. In this work, we address this ``curse of dimensionality'' by presenting a new DP synthetic data algorithm, SPLICE, that comes with a compelling global distributional guarantee, even in high-dimensions, and moreover, is practically state-of-the-art. Our algorithm is based on measuring noisy sliced Chebyshev polynomial moments of the target distribution and fitting a distribution to match, a twist on recent polynomial methods for 1-D synthetic data. We prove that, given a dataset of $n$ examples, SPLICE returns a private distribution with Sliced Wasserstein-1 distance $\tilde{O}(1/\sqrt{n})$ from the target, for constant privacy parameters. Notably, this bound is independent of the data dimension, $d$. Along the way, we prove a moment matching result of independent interest: for a distribution on the unit ball, matching the first $O(1/\alpha)$ Chebyshev moments along $\tilde{O}(d/\alpha^2)$ random directions guarantees $\alpha$ Sliced Wasserstein error. Finally, we provide a practical implementation of the algorithm that borrows tools from the tensor decomposition literature and achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to prior DP synthetic data methods on an extensive benchmark.
item.dc:creator: Lucas Rosenblatt, R. Teal Witter, Christopher Musco

item.title: Eroding the Truth-Default: A Causal Analysis of Human Susceptibility to Foundation Model Hallucinations and Disinformation in the Wild
item.description: arXiv:2601.22871v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As foundation models (FMs) approach human-level fluency, distinguishing synthetic from organic content has become a key challenge for Trustworthy Web Intelligence. This paper presents JudgeGPT and RogueGPT, a dual-axis framework that decouples "authenticity" from "attribution" to investigate the mechanisms of human susceptibility. Analyzing 918 evaluations across five FMs (including GPT-4 and Llama-2), we employ Structural Causal Models (SCMs) as a principal framework for formulating testable causal hypotheses about detection accuracy. Contrary to partisan narratives, we find that political orientation shows a negligible association with detection performance ($r=-0.10$). Instead, "fake news familiarity" emerges as a candidate mediator ($r=0.35$), suggesting that exposure may function as adversarial training for human discriminators. We identify a "fluency trap" where GPT-4 outputs (HumanMachineScore: 0.20) bypass Source Monitoring mechanisms, rendering them indistinguishable from human text. These findings suggest that "pre-bunking" interventions should target cognitive source monitoring rather than demographic segmentation to ensure trustworthy information ecosystems.

item.title: Identifying Body Composition Measures That Correlate with Self-Compassion and Social Support
item.description: arXiv:2602.18467v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This study explores the relationship between body composition metrics, self-compassion, and social support among college students. Using seasonal body composition data from the InBody770 system and psychometric measures from the Lived Experiences Measured Using Rings Study (LEMURS) (n=156; freshmen=66, sophomores=90), Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) reveals body composition metrics exhibit moderate correlation with self-compassion and social support. Certain physiological and psychological features showed strong and consistent relationships with well-being across the academic year. Trunk and leg impedance stood out as key physiological indicators, while mindfulness, over-identification, affectionate support, and tangible support emerged as recurring psychological and social correlates. This demonstrates that body composition metrics can serve as valuable biomarkers for indicating self-perceived psychosocial well-being, offering insights for future research on scalable mental health modeling and intervention strategies.
item.dc:creator: Enerson Poon, Mikaela Irene Fudolig, Johanna E. Hidalgo, Bryn C. Loftness, Kathryn Stanton, Connie L. Tompkins, Laura S. P. Bloomfield, Matthew Price, Peter Sheridan Dodds, Christopher M. Danforth, Nick Cheney

item.title: Causal Analysis of Author Demographics in Academic Peer Review
item.description: arXiv:2603.06641v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Academic meritocracy is jeopardized by systematic imbalances; for example, whereas Black and Hispanic individuals constitute over 30% of the U.S. population, they represent fewer than 10% of tenured academics in science and engineering. Peer review serves as a crucial gatekeeper in this process, however it encounters ongoing issues over biases that may hinder scientific advancement. The issue is now exacerbated by the growing influence of artificial intelligence (AI) in academic assessment. This paper transcends correlation to quantitatively assess the independent impacts of author demographics, including race, gender, and country of affiliation, on paper acceptance rankings. We utilize a causal inference methodology on a dataset of 530 papers, simulating the academic selection process by employing the prestige of the publication venue as a surrogate for review rank. Our research indicates statistically substantial causal disadvantages for authors from minority racial groups (average treatment effects [ATE]: -0.42 points in ranking), female authors (ATE: -0.25), and those associated with institutions in the Global South (ATE: -0.57). The exhibited biases emphasize the pressing necessity for fairness interventions in both conventional and AI-based review processes, indicating that such measures are essential for establishing a more equitable and credible scientific environment.
item.dc:creator: Uttamasha Anjally Oyshi, Gibson Nkhata, Susan Gauch

item.title: Can Humans Tell? A Dual-Axis Study of Human Perception of LLM-Generated News
item.description: arXiv:2604.03755v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Can humans tell whether a news article was written by a person or a large language model (LLM)? We investigate this question using JudgeGPT, a study platform that independently measures source attribution (human vs. machine) and authenticity judgment (legitimate vs. fake) on continuous scales. From 2,318 judgments collected from 1,054 participants across content generated by six LLMs, we report five findings: (1) participants cannot reliably distinguish machine-generated from human-written text (p > .05, Welch's t-test); (2) this inability holds across all tested models, including open-weight models with as few as 7B parameters; (3) self-reported domain expertise predicts judgment accuracy (r = .35, p < .001) whereas political orientation does not (r = -.10, n.s.); (4) clustering reveals distinct response strategies ("Skeptics" vs. "Believers"); and (5) accuracy degrades after approximately 30 sequential evaluations due to cognitive fatigue. The answer, in short, is no: humans cannot reliably tell. These results indicate that user-side detection is not a viable defense and motivate system-level countermeasures such as cryptographic content provenance.

item.title: A Cross-Country Evaluation of Sentiment Toward Digital Payment Systems in Africa
item.description: arXiv:2604.11566v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Digital payment systems are a cornerstone of African consumer finance, including money transfer applications, mobile money, cryptocurrencies, stablecoins, and central bank digital currencies (CBDCs). While many studies explore how people use digital payment systems (in Africa and beyond), little is known about how people choose and reason about categories of payment systems. We conducted qualitative interviews in three African countries--Nigeria, Tanzania, and Zimbabwe--to understand how and why people use various payment systems. Our study suggests that users navigate accounts and payments on multiple payment systems through a complex selection process based on perceived tradeoffs between utility, privacy, and security. Many users trust government issuers to protect them from scams, but they do not trust those same institutions to build reliable products or prioritize customer satisfaction. Our findings suggest compelling directions for regulators and the research community to design systems that balance users' trust and utility needs.

item.title: From Needs Assessment to Legal-Digital Empowerment: A Community-Based Framework for Indigenous Enterprises in Higher Education Extension Programs
item.description: arXiv:2610.38030v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: IPOs contribute significantly to local economies, cultural preservation, and sustainable livelihoods within their ancestral communities. However, many IPOs remain marginalized in digital economies due to limited digital competencies, inadequate access to technology, and insufficient legal awareness related to online enterprise participation. This study examined the marketing practices, digital competencies, and legal-literacy needs of IPOs in the Philippines and developed a legal-digital empowerment framework for higher education extension and community engagement initiatives. Using a sequential mixed-methods design, data were collected through surveys and focus group discussions involving IPO members engaged in community-based enterprises. The study assessed existing marketing practices, identified competency and legal-awareness gaps, and determined capacity-building needs related to digital enterprise participation. Findings revealed that IPOs continue to rely heavily on traditional marketing channels, with limited use of digital platforms, inconsistent branding practices, and minimal engagement in strategic digital marketing activities. Participants also expressed concerns regarding intellectual property protection, online participation, and limited understanding of legal mechanisms related to digital enterprise engagement. Despite these limitations, IPO members showed strong willingness to participate in training and mentorship initiatives. The study proposes the Legal-Digital Empowerment Framework for Indigenous Community Enterprises, which integrates digital competencies, legal literacy, institutional support systems, and rights-based market participation into a structured and context-responsive model for higher education extension programs.

item.title: IKTRACE: A Natural Language Processing Framework for Identifying Indigenous Knowledge Representation in Academic Literature
item.description: arXiv:2610.38186v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As artificial intelligence systems increasingly rely on vast textual data, respectful and accurate representation of Indigenous Knowledge has become critical. This paper introduces IKTRACE, a natural language processing framework for identifying, analyzing, and organizing Indigenous Knowledge representations in academic literature while adhering to Indigenous Data Sovereignty (IDsov) principles. We present a community-informed taxonomy co-developed with Inuit partners, comprising nine knowledge domains grounded in Indigenous Data Sovereignty principles. Building on this taxonomy, we implement a multi-method Knowledge identification pipeline using complementary natural language processing approaches. Outputs are integrated into a knowledge graph to support future expert and community validation. Applied to a corpus of Canadian Arctic research documents, IKTRACE demonstrated high accuracy and strong community relevance in expert validation. Our framework provides a scalable, ethically grounded foundation for Community-centered Knowledge validation and the development of Indigenous-informed AI systems.
item.dc:creator: Tara Azin, Christy Caudill, Mako Sorensen, Peter Pulsifer

item.title: Context-Specific Instruction: A Longitudinal Study on Debugging Skill Acquisition and Retention for Novice Programmers
item.description: arXiv:2509.22420v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Bug localization is a critical skill, yet novices often lack systematic approaches. Prior work tested abstract guidelines and general concrete steps; the impact of context-specific instruction is unclear. We ran an eight-week longitudinal study with four conditions: no instruction (G1), abstract guidelines (G2), concrete steps (G3), and our context-specific instruction that pairs concrete bug-localization steps with problem-specific details (G4). Forty-four undergraduates participated; 41 completed all five sessions (S1-S5). Each session included 2-3 debugging tasks to identify the minimal code element containing a seeded logical fault. We measured correctness (binary), time to completion, self-perceived scores (stress, difficulty, satisfaction, and strategy adherence). G4 achieved higher correctness and shorter time to completion: it reached 80% correctness after one session (vs. 20-44% for other groups) and maintained 80% after three weeks, outperforming all groups (p < 0.05); its time to completion stabilized at 13-15 minutes in S1, whereas other groups took 2-3 sessions to stabilize at 22-27 minutes. Qualitative responses showed lower stress and higher satisfaction in G4, with participants internalizing strategies via contextual examples. We conclude that context-specific instruction yields faster skill acquisition and stronger retention than abstract guidelines or context-agnostic steps. Even 1-2 sessions produced significant gains, while extended practice optimized and stabilized performance. Integrating contextual examples with abstract principles may bridge theory-practice gaps in bug-localization education and provide a more equitable path for novices.
item.dc:creator: Ziyi Zhang, Devjeet Roy, Venera Arnaoudova

item.title: Expected Harm: Rethinking Safety Evaluation of (Mis)Aligned LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2602.01600v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Current evaluations of LLM safety predominantly rely on severity-based taxonomies to assess the harmfulness of models' responses to malicious queries. We argue that this formulation requires re-examination as it implicitly equates model output with realized harm while neglecting Execution Likelihood-the conditional probability of a threat being realized by a real-world actor given a model's response. In this work, we introduce Expected Harm, a metric that weights the severity of a jailbreak by its execution likelihood, modeled as a function of execution cost. Through empirical analysis of state-of-the-art models, we reveal a systematic Inverse Risk Calibration: models disproportionately exhibit stronger refusal behaviors for low-likelihood (high-cost) threats while remaining vulnerable to high-likelihood (low-cost) queries. Mechanistically, we first provide an analysis using linear probing, revealing that while refusal mechanisms linearly separate queries by severity, they do not use execution likelihood as an indicator for refusal. Then, we use Olmo-3's open-source staged checkpoints to trace the root cause of miscalibration to the Supervised Fine Tuning (SFT) training data distribution (82.8% of safety examples at cost levels 0-1) and show that cost representations are weak from the SFT stage onward. Finally, we demonstrate that this miscalibration creates a vulnerability: by exploiting this property, we increase the attack success rate of existing jailbreaks by up to $2\times$.
item.dc:creator: Yen-Shan Chen, Zhi Rui Tam, Cheng-Kuang Wu, Yun-Nung Chen

item.title: ORACLE: Anticipating Scams from Partial Trajectories in Streaming App Usage
item.description: arXiv:2605.16363v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Smartphone scams are increasingly prevalent and typically manifest as multi-stage, cross-application processes with gradually emerging intent. Effective intervention thus requires anticipating scams before the intent becomes explicit. This is inherently challenging, as decisions must rely on partial trajectories with temporally distributed evidence. In this paper, we propose \textbf{ORACLE} Online Reasoning for Anticipating Cross-temporal Latent thrEats, the first agentic framework for early scam anticipation from \textit{streaming app-usage} trajectories. To support this setting, we curate a real-world long-horizon benchmark of streaming app-usage trajectories, covering 12 scam types, spanning extended periods (15 days on average), involving diverse applications (95 apps), and interleaving normal and scam behaviors. To address fragmented evidence, we introduce a self-evolving context manager that adaptively consolidates entity-centric interactions over time, enabling more effective reconstruction of cross-temporal evidence from partial observations. To enhance sensitivity to latent early-stage signals, we propose an on-policy self-distillation scheme in which a teacher model, conditioned on summarized anti-scam reflections and clues by skills, supervises a student model without access to such reflections. This scheme thereby distills evidence-informed knowledge and improves recognition of emerging fraud patterns from partial trajectories. Experiments show that \method{} consistently improves early scam anticipation, yielding timely warnings while reducing false alerts in realistic streaming scenarios.
item.dc:creator: Wenbo Gao, Songbai Tan, Zhongan Wang, Fei Shen, Gang Xu, Huiping Zhuang, Yunyun Yang, Ming Li, Xiaofeng Zhu

item.title: Geometry of Relaxed Fair Regression: A Unified Framework for Aware and Unaware Settings
item.description: arXiv:2605.28233v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Fairness-accuracy trade-offs are a central concern in the deployment of fairness-aware machine learning methods. When sensitive attributes are unavailable at inference time-the so called unawareness setting, principled methods for obtaining accurate predictions under relaxed fairness constraints are largely missing. In this work, we address this gap by formulating regression under a demographic parity penalty as an optimal transport problem. Our framework, unifies both the aware and unaware settings and characterizes optimal prediction functions via optimal transport maps, under both squared Wasserstein-2 and Total Variation penalties. These results reveal that the choice of penalty reflects fundamentally different fairness philosophies: the Wasserstein penalty induces a smooth, population-wide compromise, while Total Variation enforces parity for a subset of individuals. Building on these theoretical characterizations, we propose FAUST, an algorithm that is simple to implement, computationally efficient, and consistently matches or outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on real-world benchmarks.
item.dc:creator: Marie Generali Lince, Vincent Divol, R\'emi Flamary, Solenne Gaucher, Patrick Loiseau

item.title: Low-vocality Engagement and Participation Dynamics on Bluesky
item.description: arXiv:2606.21665v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Online participation is often measured through visible expression, especially posting, yet many consequential forms of engagement occur through less vocal actions such as liking and following. Here we study how users inhabit Bluesky by reconstructing participation profiles from more than three billion activity records produced by a near-complete sample accounting for more than 80\% of registered users. We aggregate behavior into monthly user-level observations and distinguish two dimensions that are often conflated in platform analytics: intensity, capturing how much users engage, and style, capturing how engagement is expressed across actions. We find that vocal production is highly concentrated, but low-posting behavior does not imply absence from platform participation. High-intensity engagement is most strongly associated with liking rather than posting, while posting-oriented participation is more common among low-intensity users, indicating that visibility and sustained engagement should not be conflated. Transition patterns suggest that high-intensity likers and posters could be described as attractors; network-building redirects users within the active space; whereas observed inactivity acts as a persistent boundary that selectively limits re-entry. Higher-order motifs further show that inactivity often interrupts rather than erases prior regimes, and that low-intensity liking can precede durable high-intensity engagement. These results show that online participation is structured by differentiated low-vocality practices, calling for a shift from post-centered measures of activity toward dynamic accounts of platform presence. We identify a broader challenge for computational social science: platform participation cannot be adequately understood through the behavior of vocal minorities alone.
item.dc:creator: Veronica Mesina, Andrea Failla, Luca Pappalardo, Giulio Rossetti

item.title: Making Sense of Audience Change: Causal Attribution and Boundary Management on Xiaohongshu
item.description: arXiv:2610.38026v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recommendation-driven platforms can reshape not only what users see, but also who becomes visible and how community boundaries are negotiated. We examine Xiaohongshu discussions surrounding a perceived World Cup-related audience influx to understand how users attributed community change and how those explanations related to boundary-management strategies. We analyzed 262 comments from eight high-engagement threads using researcher-led thematic analysis, structured coding, and permutation-based association analysis. Users described personalization as both social separation and a boundary that could fail, interpreted platform growth through audience acquisition and commercialization, and contested whether gender should define community membership. Among 70 comments with explicit attributions and strategies, attribution and strategy were strongly associated (Cramer's V = .583): algorithmic attributions concentrated in technical boundary management, while social-actor attributions more often aligned with social enforcement or normative socialization. These findings connect causal sensemaking with boundary management and show how audience restructuring can create governance consequences on recommendation-driven platforms.
item.dc:creator: Zhiyi (Erin), Zhou, Kyrie Zhou

item.title: Infrastructure and its Discontents: Contestations of Power in Canada's AI Governance Scaffold
item.description: arXiv:2610.38077v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper develops a critical theoretical framework for understanding national Artificial Intelligence (AI) strategies through the lens of "Governance as Infrastructure." Integrating insights from Infrastructure Studies, Science and Technology Studies (STS), this paper employs Black Feminist Technoscience (BFTS) to reveal how AI governance infrastructures are assembled, maintained, and contested, and whose forms of knowledge, labour, and experience are rendered visible or invisible in these processes. We analyze the Canadian AI governance landscape through in-depth interviews with bureaucrats, civil society advocacy groups, academic researchers, and industry actors. Our inductive thematic analysis reveals how AI governance infrastructure enacts specific configurations of power, particularly through the politics of expertise; how actors navigate profound ambiguities related to AI's opacity, often involving strategic ignorance; and how mechanisms for justice and accountability struggle to address AI-related harms. We contend that a BFTS perspective highlights the limitations of current governance approaches and points toward alternative infrastructural designs prioritizing care, maintenance, participatory democracy, and adaptive temporalities to foster more equitable and accountable technology governance.
item.dc:creator: Christelle Tessono, Nusrat Jahan Mim, Shion Guha

item.title: Robustness of Chatbot LLM Judgments of Presidential Actions and Hypothetical Reforms
item.description: arXiv:2610.39398v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Chatbots are increasingly consulted about public affairs, and their judgments of policies are useful only if they are robust. We measure this robustness in the setting of an ordinary user, through consumer chat interfaces. For 30 days, five chatbot configurations (Mistral, Gemini Flash, Claude Sonnet, and Claude Opus at two effort settings) were asked twice a day to score the long-term effect on the United States of 40 actions of the last four presidential administrations and of 15 hypothetical reforms, each with a confidence and a short comment. The judgments are robust: all configurations agree on the sign and the ranking of the administrations' mean scores, and two different configurations asked on the same day give opposite signs to the same action in about 4% of cases. Responses from different days differ more than same-day responses (which shared the order of the items); the difference grows slowly over the month, except where the service itself changed. We identify three such changes, which shifted the judgments while leaving little or no trace in the interface. Treating the comments as a retrieval task, we find them specific to each item and consistent across runs and chatbots, with lexical and embedding similarities agreeing. We release the dataset of 16,500 judgments.
item.dc:creator: Oleg Vasilyev
